extracted.intended_audience: magazine readers and journalism professionals (editors, reporters, fact-checkers)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for verifying, publishing, and — if necessary — retracting first-person/magazine pieces, especially those using anonymity and wartime sources. Emphasizes independent verification, conflict-of-interest avoidance, transparency with readers, and thresholds for standing by or retracting stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking (independent verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking is a process used by most magazines (but not most newspapers) to independently verify what's in their articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent verification rather than relying solely on the author's account; seek corroborating testimony, contemporaneous documents, and other evidence that can confirm factual claims. Recognize that fact-checking is especially crucial for extraordinary or sensitive anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest in fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: His wife, Reeve, was assigned a large role in checking his third piece... there was a clear conflict of interest. It was a mistake—and we've imposed new rules to prevent future fact-checking conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assign close personal relationships (spouses, intimate friends, people with existing personal ties) to verify an author's work. Implement rules to prevent such conflicts and reassign verification tasks to independent staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance protecting anonymity with need to verify
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we promised to protect his identity, we were reluctant to call Army public affairs to review his claims. His anonymity complicated this process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When granting anonymity, establish verification pathways that do not compromise source protection. Weigh the obligation to protect the writer against editorial responsibility to independently verify key factual claims—seek alternatives such as off-the-record confirmations, third-party corroboration, or controlled disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek easily verifiable benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: We searched for the easily verifiable bits of information that would serve as crucial benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and confirm small, verifiable facts (dates, locations, employment history, contemporaneous emails, photos, official records) that anchor a first-person narrative. These benchmarks help assess credibility of less-verifiable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on the author's word for first-person narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact-checking of first-person articles about personal experiences necessarily relies heavily on the author’s word and description of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that first-person pieces depend on the author's testimony, but require additional corroboration where possible (witnesses, documents, physical evidence). Treat lone assertions, especially extraordinary ones, with skepticism until independently corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer admission of error over concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: If you got anything wrong or exaggerated things, people will understand; it's better to admit error than get caught in a lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authors to acknowledge mistakes proactively. Editorially, favor transparent corrections or clarifications rather than allowing uncorrected inaccuracies to persist and later be exposed as deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to readers about investigative process
rubrics_metrics.description: When these accusations first arose, we promised our readers a full account of our investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish a clear account of how the newsroom investigated allegations, what evidence was sought, what was found, and what remains unresolved. Transparency helps maintain trust even when conclusions are inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for standing by vs retracting a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Without that essential confidence, we cannot stand by these stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require editorial confidence that events occurred 'in the manner described' before standing by published first-person accounts. If independent corroboration is insufficient and key facts are in doubt, consider correction or retraction per established editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of anonymity for inexperienced writers
rubrics_metrics.description: He was a young soldier in a war zone, an untried writer without journalistic training. We published his accounts... granting him the shield of anonymity—which, in the wrong hands, can become license to exaggerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially cautious granting anonymity to inexperienced or unvetted writers for sensitive topics; anonymity can facilitate exaggeration. Apply stricter verification before publishing such anonymous first-person pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on witnesses solicited by the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of these contacts wasn't ideal: Beauchamp was soliciting his own witnesses. But, once Beauchamp established the initial contact, we tried to communicate with these soldiers independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer witnesses identified independently by reporters rather than those recruited by the subject; if the subject supplies witnesses, independently re-interview and corroborate their accounts to reduce risk of coordinated narratives or cover-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value contemporaneous notes/emails/photos as reporter evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reeve provided us with a contemporaneous e-mail from him that described the same event. Beauchamp wasn’t a reporter, but these served the same function as a reporter’s notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat contemporaneous communications, notes, and photos as strong forms of evidence. Seek and preserve such materials to corroborate timeline and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult subject-matter experts for plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: We sent the piece to a correspondent for a major newspaper who had spent many tours embedded in Iraq... we called a forensic anthropologist and a spokesman for the manufacturer of Bradley Fighting Vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounts involve technical, military, or forensic details, consult qualified experts to assess plausibility and interpret physical/technical claims (e.g., whether a vehicle could cause a described injury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider an author's prior writings and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: We discovered his blog... With his excited prose and tendency toward overstatement, his blog did not inspire journalistic confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review an author's prior public writing and behavior for patterns (exaggeration, melodrama, fabrication) that could affect credibility. Use such context in editorial risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain official documents and pursue FOIA where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: We've asked for sworn statements that the military had him draft and sign... the four months and counting it has taken to process our Freedom of Information Act request for those results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue official records, sworn statements, and public documents (including FOIA requests) to corroborate or refute contested claims. Track and disclose delays or lack of cooperation from authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about relying on statements made under duress or with supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: He spoke on speakerphone... he refused to even talk about his stories with us. Beauchamp said he might want to publish another statement standing by his story. He spoke under duress... statements he made to us had seemed unusually formulaic and coached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statements made in the presence of superiors, under pressure, or after coercion as potentially unreliable; seek corroboration and avoid using such statements as definitive retractions or confirmations without independent evidence.
